summary: Christian Island Light, first shown 1 May 1859 on Georgian Bay: the Hoars and two more head keepers, a 1906 loss off Cape Croker, discontinued 1922, Coast Guard light today.

lens.note: Fourth-order Fresnel lens with argand lamp, lantern and apparatus from the Paris firm of Louis Sautter (LighthouseFriends)

structures.note: Tower and keeper's dwelling finished 1856 except the lantern (LighthouseFriends; Anishinabek News); plaque text gives 1857; Lighthouse Directory gives 1859 (John Brown). Height given as 17.5 m (Coast Guard list), 18.5 m / 61 ft (Lighthouse Directory), 55 ft to centre of light (LighthouseFriends)
One-and-a-half-storey stone keepers house in ruins (Lighthouse Directory); remnants of the exterior block wall still visible (Anishinabek News)

access.note: Island is a reserve of the Beausoleil First Nation, reached by passenger ferry from Cedar Point; grounds open, tower closed (LighthouseFriends; Lighthouse Directory)

events.note: Builder John Brown of Thorold contracted for eleven lighthouses; six built
Tower and keeper's dwelling finished save the lantern (LighthouseFriends; Anishinabek News). Plaque gives 1857
Treaty of 29 March 1857: ten acres at Bar Point surrendered for lighthouse purposes (Anishinabek News)
Fixed white light from its fourth-order Fresnel lens first displayed on 1 May 1859
Keeper William Hoar complained of a garden fence torn down; Superintendent D. G. Smith met the Assance Band on 16 December 1863
Pre-confederate Treaty No. 120 agreed at Christian Island on 26 June 1866, adding land for the light (Anishinabek News)
John Hoar took charge of the light on his father's retirement
Inspection by Darius Smith, Superintendent of Lights above Montreal, found the wall cracked from top to bottom
Breastwork protection with groins built at a cost of $213.20
Allan Collins head keeper from 1891; John Hoar swapped positions with the keeper of Hope Island Lighthouse
Steamer J. H. Jones lost off Cape Croker; wreckage came ashore at Christian Island (see wrecks)
Duplex lamp replaced by a 35 mm. Diamond vapour installation and adjustable brass stand (Department of Marine report for the fiscal year ended 31 March 1909, printed 1910)
Tug Saucy Jim totally destroyed by fire while lying at Christian Island on 25 November 1910
Discontinued 1 April 1922 after an offshore buoy replaced it
Coast Guard placed a beacon showing a white flash every four seconds on the tower
Lantern room re-established on the tower; LighthouseFriends says early 2000s, Lighthouse Directory around 2000, Anishinabek News the turn of the century
Huronia Lightstation Preservation Society marked the 150th anniversary with a plaque

notes_for_editor: Construction and first light: the sources disagree on when the tower was finished. Anishinabek News says 1856 (lighthouse and keeper's home completed); LighthouseFriends says essentially finished in 1856 but its 2007 plaque text says constructed in 1857; Lighthouse Directory says 1859 (John Brown). The story gives all three and does not choose. First light 1 May 1859 is in both LighthouseFriends and Anishinabek News. The record's built 1859 (from Rowlett) is left as is; the editor may want to revise it. Focal height: LighthouseFriends 61 ft above water (18.6 m); Lighthouse Directory 19.5 m (64 ft); Coast Guard list 20.2 m (record value). Tower height: 55 ft to centre of light (LF), 18.5 m / 61 ft (Rowlett), 17.5 m (CCG), 60-ft in Anishinabek News. The story reports the spread. Keepers: names and years come from LighthouseFriends's 'Head Keepers' line and the same years in Anishinabek News (John H. Hoar, Captain William Hoar). Department of Marine tables for 1912-1915 print 'T. Marchildon (lightkeeper)' and 'A. Collins' in OCR column blocks, next to an engineer and other stations; I could not tie these lines to Christian Island from the text, so they are not cited. A human should check the page images (identifiers 1913v47i15p21_0943 scan 78, 1914v48i16p21_1031 scan 83, 1915v50i16p21_1119 scans 74 and 75, 1916v51i17p21_1196 scan 86) before relying on them. The 1907 wreck report's period is taken from the volume's own words ('nine months ended March 31 last'), so the year 1907 is inferred from that phrase and the 1906 date of the wreck. The Imperial Towers (John Brown, 1855 contract) are also a story in this batch for Griffith Island; LighthouseFriends lists Griffith Island among the six towers. Thomas Patterson (keeper of Cape Beale, married to Minnie Huff) is named in LighthouseFriends only as a connection by marriage and is not put on any roster; the editor may link the Cape Beale record. The Parks Canada heritage record for the tower (page id 4464, search snippet: built 1855 to 1859 by John Brown) is not cited: the cached copy is an empty stub. Huronia Lightstation Preservation Society plaque: only the event is cited, the wording of the plaque comes from LighthouseFriends. Not checked: Commissioners of Public Works annual reports (quoted in LighthouseFriends, not in the corpus) and the Treaty No. 120 text. The 1878 Darius Smith quotation and the 1887 breastwork cost are as LighthouseFriends prints them from the official report; no page number is given there. The 1906 wreck is reported in the Marine annual report with no rescue at the island; no newspaper search was made: Chronicling America is a US archive and does not cover Ontario papers. The 2007 plaque text, as printed by LighthouseFriends, reads 'Constructed in 1857'. The CCG list shows the Christian Island light with the entry remark 'Seasonal (in place year round)'; the story does not use the word seasonal. Access: the island is a Beausoleil First Nation reserve, reached by passenger ferry from Cedar Point; the record's access was 'unknown' and is set to 'restricted' here.
